subject: Business
title: Unit Economics: The Health Check
description: A micro-lesson that makes Unit Economics: The Health Check usable.

hook.text: Your startup grows 10% monthly. Impressive — until you realize you lose $3 on every sale.

buildup.text: Unit economics measures whether each transaction makes or loses money before overhead.

discovery.text: Customer lifetime value vs. acquisition cost is the core equation: LTV vs. CAC.

twist.text: Many startups grow by subsidizing each sale. That works until investors stop writing checks.

climax.text: A healthy ratio is LTV to CAC of 3:1 — earn three dollars for every one spent acquiring.

punchline.text: Revenue means nothing if every sale costs more than it earns.

quiz.question: What is a healthy LTV:CAC ratio?

details.summary: Unit economics measure the revenue and cost associated with a single customer or unit, determining whether a business can be profitable at scale. If the lifetime value of a customer exceeds the cost to acquire them by a healthy margin, the business model is fundamentally sound.
details.whyItMatters: Many startups grow rapidly while losing money on every customer, hoping to fix economics at scale. Unit economics reveals whether growth is creating or destroying value, providing the fundamental health check that determines long-term viability.
takeaways: Customer lifetime value must exceed acquisition cost by at least three to one
Unit economics determine whether growth creates value or accelerates losses
Profitable unit economics are the foundation of sustainable business growth

faq.question: What is a healthy LTV to CAC ratio?
faq.answer: Generally three to one or higher is considered healthy. Below three to one suggests either acquisition is too expensive or retention is too low. Above five to one may suggest under-investment in growth. The ratio should be calculated on a cohort basis to track trends over time.

faq.question: Can a company with poor unit economics grow into profitability?
faq.answer: Sometimes, if scale genuinely reduces costs or increases revenue per customer. Network effects may reduce acquisition costs over time. But hoping to fix unit economics at scale without a specific mechanism is a common startup trap. Identify exactly what will change and by how much.
